newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African fuel prices seen lower in months ahead.
newsitem.headline: S.African fuel prices seen lower in months ahead.

text.p: Lower international oil prices and a stronger rand are expected to result in lower South African fuel prices in the months ahead, while also providing relief on the inflation front, economists said on Wednesday.
Oil prices have fallen from around $22.50 a barrel at the start of the year to its current $18.50 a barrel, while at the same time the rand has stregthened from 4.70 rand to the dollar to 4.44 rand.
That has resulted in three cent reduction in the retail gasoline price so far this year to its current 221 cents a litre around Johannesburg and a 26 cent reduction in the diesel price to 200 cents.
EW Balderson economist Mike Schussler said he expected the recent downward trend in local gasoline and diesel prices to continue into the second half of this year.

"I think we are going to see a downward trend in general in the petrol and diesel prices for the next four or five months until we get to August when people start buying oil for the northern winter," Schussler said, adding that he expected the petrol price to average between 210 to 220 cents a litre over that period.
However, gasoline prices could fall even further, given the outlook for international oil prices in the second half.

"The outlook for oil prices is pretty gloomy, particularly in the second half of the year and the main reason is that supplies are building up because non-Opec output is accelerating and the days of Opec cutting production are finished," Geoff Payne, Union Bank of Switzerland's (UBS) oil analyst, said.
"What you have is coming up for one million barrels a day of oversupply in the second half. That has been hidden from the market so far this year because inventories started out the year so low."
He said UBS' forecast for Brent in the second half, which was last trading at around $18.25 a barrel, was currently under downward revision.
"If it does get revised down we are looking at a $16.50 to $17.50 a barrel range for the second half," Payne said.
UBS emerging markets analyst Constantin Vayenas saad he expected falling local fuel prices to help South African consumer inflation back to the 7.5 percent mark by December.

"Compared to the end of last year, international oil prices have fallen by about 25 to 30 percent. Given that the rand has appreciated by about six percent over the same period, it is a double benefit for the country," he said.
"It is one of the key factors for inflation. Although it has a fairly low weighting in the (inflation) basket, it affects other areas as well," Vayenas said.

Vayenas said that coupled with other technical factors, such as the reduced impact of last year's mortgage rate hike, as well as his forecast for two one percentage point rate cuts this year, inflation could be reduced significantly by year-end.
"By year-end a year-on-year figure of 7.5 percent is realistic, which will push up the year average to 8.9 percent," he said.
Consumer inflation rose 9.6 percent year-on-year in March, the latest figure available, and averaged 7.4 percent for the whole of 1996.

On Friday, the Central Energy Fund is expected to announce that May's petrol price, which the Fund sets on a monthly basis, will remain unchanged following a 0.381 cent under-recovery in the price this month.
Diesel is expected to be hiked by six cents a litre, although economists said this was largely a result of a statistical glitch following a strong over-recovery in February.
